title: Databases: SQL & NoSQL
requirement: Strong knowledge of relational and non-relational databases: schema design, query optimization, data persistence.

questions.question: How do you decide between a relational and a non-relational database for a service?
questions.answer: I let access patterns and consistency needs decide. If I need constraints, ACID and ad-hoc joins across normalized data, I stay relational. For key lookups, append-heavy feeds or huge write volume, I go NoSQL and accept eventual consistency.
questions.keyTakeaway: Let access patterns and consistency needs pick the engine, not the trend.

diagram.title: Relational or non-relational
diagram.condition: Joins across normalized entities, or strict consistency needed?

questions.question: When do you normalize and when do you denormalize a schema?
questions.answer: I normalize so each fact lives in one place. I denormalize on purpose for a hot read, duplicating data to kill a join, and every copy needs a refresh plan. I decide per query, not per database.
questions.keyTakeaway: Normalize for write integrity; denormalize per hot read, with a refresh plan.

questions.question: How does a B-tree index speed up queries, and what does it cost?
questions.answer: A B-tree keeps keys sorted, so a lookup descends a few pages instead of scanning, and ranges walk adjacent leaves. The catch is every write maintains every index, plus storage and cache. So I index what queries filter, join and sort on.
questions.keyTakeaway: Indexes buy log-time lookups and range scans; they tax every write.

questions.question: Why does column order matter in a compound index?
questions.answer: An index on (a, b) serves queries on a, or a and b, but not b alone. So equality columns go first, then one range column, since nothing after a range can seek. I check the plan.
questions.keyTakeaway: Equality columns first, range last; the plan confirms the index is used.

questions.question: A query got slow in production. Walk through your optimization process.
questions.answer: I read the execution plan to see where time goes: scans, joins, sorts or waits. Then I check for a missing index, a function around an indexed column, or stale statistics. I fix the query shape before settings, and re-measure.
questions.keyTakeaway: Read the plan, fix the shape, add indexes deliberately, re-measure.

questions.question: Explain ACID and what isolation levels trade away.
questions.answer: Atomicity is all-or-nothing, consistency means constraints hold, isolation hides concurrent transactions, durability means commits survive a crash. Serializable is safest but costs throughput. Weaker levels allow anomalies like write skew. I pick the weakest my logic tolerates and retry on conflict.
questions.keyTakeaway: Isolation level is a throughput-versus-anomalies dial; retry on conflict.

questions.question: How do replication and sharding differ, and when do you need each?
questions.answer: Replication copies data to more nodes for read capacity and availability, but writes still hit one primary. Sharding splits data by a key like user id, which scales writes and storage, but cross-shard queries and resharding hurt. I replicate first and shard only when one machine can't cope.
questions.keyTakeaway: Replication scales reads; sharding scales writes and storage at high operational cost.

questions.question: You add a cache in front of the database. How do you keep it from serving stale data?
questions.answer: I decide how stale each data type may be. Cache-aside with a TTL is my default, plus invalidation on write for hot entities. I coalesce requests so one expired key causes one reload, not a stampede.
questions.keyTakeaway: TTL for safety, write-through invalidation for freshness, coalescing against stampedes.

questions.question: Two users reserve the last available room at the same time. How do you prevent a double booking?
questions.answer: Check-then-update is a race, because both transactions read the same inventory and commit. For one user double-clicking, I use a client-generated reservation id with a unique constraint. For concurrent users, the cheapest fix is a conditional update that re-checks availability in the statement itself. Under heavy contention I'd use SELECT FOR UPDATE.
questions.keyTakeaway: Push the invariant into the update; idempotency keys stop double clicks.

code.snippet:
-- atomic: updates 0 rows when the cap is exceeded, no read-then-write race
UPDATE room_type_inventory
SET total_reserved = total_reserved + $rooms
WHERE hotel_id = $hotel AND room_type_id = $type
  AND date BETWEEN $start AND $end
  AND total_reserved + $rooms <= total_inventory * 1.1; -- 10% overbooking allowed
-- rows_updated < nights requested means the reservation must be rejected

questions.question: How would you design a distributed key-value store that stays available and scales horizontally?
questions.answer: I'd partition with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, and replicate each key to N nodes across data centers. Quorums tune consistency: with W write acks and R read replicas, W plus R greater than N guarantees overlap, and N=3, W=R=2 is common. Vector clocks flag conflicting versions for the client to reconcile. That's the Dynamo model, AP with tunable consistency.
questions.keyTakeaway: Consistent-hash partitions, N replicas, quorum W+R>N, vector clocks for conflicts.

rows.label: Consistency
rows.note: W plus R greater than N

questions.question: When would you partition a large table, and how do you choose the strategy?
questions.answer: I partition when maintenance gets painful, like hour-long vacuums or index builds, old data is rarely touched, and queries filter on date or tenant. Range by time is my default, because retention becomes dropping a partition instead of a giant DELETE. It only pays off if the partition key is in the WHERE, so the planner can prune.
questions.keyTakeaway: Partition on the axis your queries filter, or the planner will scan every partition.

diagram.title: Partition pruning
diagram.condition: Does the plan filter on the partition key?

questions.question: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY, and when do you reach for them?
questions.answer: GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group and loses the detail. Window functions compute over a partition but keep every row, so I can show a running total or a rank beside each order. They replace self-joins and correlated subqueries. They run after aggregation, so to filter on one I wrap it in a subquery or CTE.
questions.keyTakeaway: Window functions aggregate over rows while keeping them, no self-join required.

code.snippet:
-- rank sellers in region, running total per seller; rows are kept, not collapsed
SELECT region, seller, month, amount,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) AS region_rank,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month) AS running_total
FROM monthly_sales
WHERE month >= DATE '2026-01-01';
-- need to filter on region_rank? wrap the query in a CTE first

questions.question: What is a covering index, and when is it worth the extra write cost?
questions.answer: A covering index holds every column a query needs, so the engine answers from the index without touching the table. That's an index-only scan. I use it on hot read paths, with INCLUDE for payload columns. The cost is bigger indexes and more write overhead, so I cover only the top queries and check the plan.
questions.keyTakeaway: A covering index answers without touching the table, verified by an index-only scan.

questions.question: How do you size a database connection pool for a busy service?
questions.answer: Every connection is a backend process with its own memory, so a Postgres box struggles long before a thousand connections, which is why we use PgBouncer. I start from the server's cores, roughly cores times 2 per instance, then divide across replicas. I tune with pool wait time and set acquisition timeouts so saturation fails fast.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pool size comes from the server's core budget, split across replicas, tuned with wait metrics.

questions.question: A query plan flipped overnight with no code change — what happened and how do you respond?
questions.answer: Something in the inputs changed: stale or skewed statistics after a bulk load, a parameter crossing a selectivity cliff, or a plan cache reset by an upgrade. I compare old and new plans and the row estimates against reality. Then I refresh statistics, fix the query shape or add an index, and only last use hints, which rot as data changes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Fix statistics and query shape before reaching for hints; hints are a splint that rots.

questions.question: What is change data capture, and when would you introduce it?
questions.answer: CDC turns the commit log into an event stream. A connector tails the write-ahead log and emits every committed change in order, so search indexes, caches and analytics copies converge without dual-write bugs. Debezium on Kafka is the usual stack. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent. I adopt it when several consumers need the same changes.
questions.keyTakeaway: CDC streams the commit log once, in order, and kills dual-write drift.

questions.question: How do deadlocks happen and how do you design them out of a system?
questions.answer: A deadlock is two transactions each holding a lock the other wants. The cure is discipline. I touch rows in one consistent order everywhere, usually primary key ascending, and keep transactions short. I never hold a lock across an external API call. And when a deadlock still happens, I just retry.
questions.keyTakeaway: Lock rows in one consistent order and keep transactions short; retry deadlocks as routine.

questions.question: Why does OFFSET pagination fall over at scale, and what replaces it?
questions.answer: OFFSET 100000 still produces and discards the first hundred thousand rows, so deep pages get slower, and shifting rows can duplicate or skip entries. Keyset pagination uses the last seen sort value, like WHERE (created_at, id) > (last_ts, last_id) LIMIT 20. It seeks the index at constant cost.
questions.keyTakeaway: Keyset pagination seeks by last-seen sort value and stays fast at any depth.

questions.question: When do you use a materialized view, and how do you keep it fresh?
questions.answer: A materialized view stores the query result, so heavy aggregations drop from seconds to milliseconds. The cost is staleness, so it suits dashboards and reports that tolerate some lag, never the write path. A scheduled REFRESH is simplest, and incremental maintenance keeps big views affordable. I measure refresh time before promising freshness.
questions.keyTakeaway: A materialized view trades refresh cost for read speed; match cadence to staleness tolerance.

questions.question: How do you choose between bigint, UUIDv4, and UUIDv7 primary keys?
questions.answer: Random UUIDv4 keys are a hidden tax: 16 bytes versus 8, and every insert lands at a random B-tree position, which thrashes the cache and bloats indexes. Bigint is smallest and fastest inside one database. UUIDv7 is time-ordered, so indexes stay compact, and it needs no coordination. I use bigint in one database and UUIDv7 for distributed or public ids.
questions.keyTakeaway: Time-ordered keys, UUIDv7 or bigint, keep inserts sequential; random UUIDv4 fragments indexes.

questions.question: Users complain their changes vanish right after saving — how do you handle replication lag and read-your-writes?
questions.answer: The write hits the primary, then the next read goes to a lagging replica and the change seems to vanish. First I reduce and monitor the lag. Then I route by need: pin a user to the primary briefly after they write, or hold their reads until the replica passes a version token from that write.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pin a user's post-write reads to the primary, or hold at the replica with version tokens.

questions.question: How do you index queries against JSON columns in Postgres?
questions.answer: I use three tools. A GIN index on jsonb handles containment queries like data @> '{"role": "admin"}', but costs write overhead and space. An expression index on one path, like (data->>'event_type'), is much cheaper when queries touch known fields. Hot JSON fields I promote to real columns. GIN is for the flexible long tail.
questions.keyTakeaway: GIN for containment over whole documents, expression indexes for known paths, columns for hot fields.

questions.question: How do you keep an append-only table from growing forever?
questions.answer: I plan the lifecycle up front: hot, cold, deletable. For pure expiry I drop old time partitions, which is instant and avoids a vacuum storm. A DELETE loop over millions of rows causes bloat and replication lag. Data worth keeping goes to object storage as Parquet first. And I test restores, because archives nobody can reload are gone.
questions.keyTakeaway: Expire by dropping partitions, archive before deleting, and always test the restore.

questions.question: How do you choose between row-level security, schema-per-tenant, and database-per-tenant?
questions.answer: Database-per-tenant isolates best but costs the most to run, since a thousand tenants means a thousand migrations. Schema-per-tenant still multiplies migrations and complicates pools. Row-level security on shared tables scales to huge tenant counts with one schema, and the engine enforces tenant_id even if app code forgets the WHERE. I start with RLS and go heavier only for contracts.
questions.keyTakeaway: Enforce tenancy in the engine with RLS; reserve schema- or db-per-tenant for contract demands.

questions.question: When do you choose optimistic versus pessimistic concurrency in the application layer?
questions.answer: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: read a version, update WHERE version = seen, retry on conflict. No locks held, but heavy contention causes retry storms. Pessimistic means SELECT FOR UPDATE, predictable on hot rows but it blocks and risks deadlocks. Carts get optimistic with bounded retries. Inventory and balances get a real lock or an atomic conditional update.
questions.keyTakeaway: Optimistic for low contention with bounded retries; lock the rows money depends on.

questions.question: How do you diagnose and fix a hot partition when one shard redlines while the rest idle?
questions.answer: A hot shard means the key correlates with traffic: monotonically increasing keys send every insert to the newest partition, or one huge tenant dominates. I spot it from per-shard query rate and lock waits. To mitigate, I salt the key with a bucket suffix, isolate the noisy tenant, or cache the hot reads. Resharding is the last resort, since hotspots re-form on a skewed key.
questions.keyTakeaway: Defuse hot shards by salting the key or isolating the noisy tenant, not by resharding blindly.

questions.question: How do you change a schema on a large table without downtime?
questions.answer: Expand, migrate, contract, and never one DDL that rewrites a live table. I add nullable columns, backfill in batches, deploy code that writes both shapes, then flip reads. Only in a later release do I drop the old columns. In Postgres I use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and I keep every step reversible behind a flag.
questions.keyTakeaway: Expand, backfill, flip, contract: never let one DDL rewrite a live table.

questions.question: How does a backup strategy turn a bad delete from an hour ago into a boring recovery?
questions.answer: Nightly full backups lose everything since midnight. I use continuous archiving: a base backup plus WAL streamed to object storage. Then point-in-time recovery lets me restore to just before the bad delete and copy back the lost rows. I run restore drills and check RPO and RTO against what the business needs.
questions.keyTakeaway: Base backup plus WAL archiving buys point-in-time recovery; rehearse restores or it is theater.
